title: The swan
hookLine: a later telling: cousin Devadatta shoots a swan, Siddhattha tends it, and the court says it belongs to the one who saved it
carry: life belongs to who protects it

cards: Two boys, cousins, in the palace gardens. A flock of swans flies overhead, white against the sky. One of the cousins has a bow.
He draws it and shoots, and a swan falls out of the sky, an arrow through its wing.

It's the last childhood story after a week of them: a queen's dream of a white elephant, a birth in a garden on the road, an old sage in tears, a mother lost at seven days and a mother who stayed, a name that's a wish, a boy at peace under a tree.
Millions of children have heard this one.

teach.b: The cousin with the bow is Devadatta. Remember that name; he'll be back, and not kindly. The swan lands near Siddhattha, who gets there first.
He kneels, gently pulls out the arrow, and holds the bird against himself to calm it, tending the wound. Devadatta runs up.
That's my swan. I shot it. Give it to me.
No, says Siddhattha. It isn't yours. You tried to kill it.
The boys can't settle it, so, the story goes, they take it to the court, to the wise men. Both sides are heard. The hunter says: I brought it down, so it's mine.
The healer says: I kept it alive, so it's in my care. The court decides: a life belongs to the one who saves it, not the one who tries to take it.
The swan goes with Siddhattha, who looks after it until it can fly, and then lets it go. To be honest about this one: it isn't in the oldest Buddhist texts.
It's a later telling, made well-known in the West by a long English poem, The Light of Asia, published by Edwin Arnold in eighteen seventy-nine.

teach.h: LIFE BELONGS TO WHO PROTECTS IT.
teach.b: But it's loved across the Buddhist world, in picture books, school plays and temple paintings, because it says something the whole tradition believes.
The first precept is not to harm living beings, and here it is in a child, before anyone taught him. And look at the judgment. Not might makes right.

how: Buddhists tell the swan story to children as an example of compassion toward animals; many Buddhists practice releasing or protecting animals, and some keep a vegetarian diet out of the same concern for living beings.

games.q: you're the wise men at court. Devadatta says: I shot it, it's mine. Siddhattha says: I saved it. who gets the swan?
games.why: the one who saved it. a life belongs to the one who protects it, not the one who tries to take it.

practice: Picture one small living thing near you: a plant, a pet, a bird at the feeder, an insect you might carry outside. See yourself tending it slowly, with the same gentle hands the boy used with the swan.
Then rest in the breath and let a little metta go to that small life.

wordCard.voice: The swan. Devadatta shot it, Siddhattha saved it, and the court said a life belongs to the one who protects it.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: a swan or goose, a common image of purity and grace in Indian traditions.

carryVoice: Your line: life belongs to who protects it. Not the hunter's: the healer's. That's week four.
